name: Whitening strips
lead: Whitening strips are thin, flexible plastic films coated with a peroxide gel that are pressed onto the front surfaces of the teeth for a set period, typically daily over one to several weeks, to lighten tooth colour. They are sold over the counter and are among the most widely used consumer tooth-whitening products.[1][2]

Peroxide bleaching works by delivering hydrogen peroxide (directly or from carbamide peroxide) that diffuses into the tooth and breaks down into reactive species that fragment pigment molecules, so that they reflect less colour.[1][3] Wikipedia reports that strips, introduced in the late 1980s, are typically applied twice daily for 30 minutes for 14 days and can lighten teeth by one or two shades within several days, depending on frequency of use and product.[1]

Reviews describe peroxide-based whitening as safe and effective when manufacturers' protocols are followed, with transient tooth sensitivity and gum irritation as the main side effects.[4][5] Randomized trials dating from 1992 onward have compared peroxide whiteners with placebo.[6]

Lightens tooth colour by roughly 1 to 2 shades in typical use[1]

paras: Strips are shaped to fit the buccal (outer) surfaces of the teeth, so they mostly cover the front teeth.[1] Related home options include paint-on whitening gels, tray-based carbamide peroxide systems worn for hours daily or overnight, whitening rinses and whitening toothpastes; the last use abrasives and sometimes low-concentration peroxide.[1] Dentist-supervised trays use higher peroxide concentrations and in-office treatments use much higher concentrations with or without light activation.[1][2]

Home whitening strips were introduced in the late 1980s, after earlier tray-based carbamide peroxide systems.[1] Aesthetic dentistry has expanded considerably over the past century, with whitening now one of the most requested cosmetic dental procedures.[7][5]

Tooth whitening is a dynamic process involving diffusion of the whitening agent, interaction with stain molecules and micromorphological changes in the tooth.[3] Extrinsic stains arise from beverages, foods, tobacco and other environmental factors, and intrinsic discolouration from ageing, wear and developmental factors; bleaching mainly targets intrinsic and deeper stains that polishing cannot remove.[1] Tooth colour perception is influenced by many factors including lighting and background, and colour science underpins its measurement.[8]

A 1992 double-blind trial reported that two carbamide peroxide products produced significantly whiter teeth than placebo after six weeks.[6] A later randomized trial compared whitening strips with a paint-on gel and a negative control.[9] A 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis compared strip use with supervised dental bleaching,[10] and a Cochrane review has examined home-based chemical bleaching in adults.[11] A 2024 review of professional whitening is also available.[12]

Reviews characterise the effect as clinically noticeable but variable, depending on stain type, product and regimen; Grokipedia states 2 to 8 shade improvements on standardised scales are reported for extrinsic stains, with intrinsic stains such as tetracycline responding more slowly or poorly.[13] Results fade gradually, and Wikipedia notes that effects of in-office whitening can last months, varying with lifestyle.[1]

Transient tooth sensitivity and gingival irritation are the most frequent side effects, usually resolving after stopping use; Grokipedia cites a range of 8 to 66 percent of users reporting sensitivity.[13][4] Wikipedia lists groups advised to use whitening with caution, including those with peroxide allergy, existing sensitive teeth, cracks or exposed dentine, enamel defects, acid erosion, gum recession, defective restorations or tooth decay, and notes that a prior oral examination is recommended.[1] Whitening does not change the colour of existing crowns or veneers.[13] Strips fit unevenly on crowded teeth, which can leave patchy coverage.

Teeth whitening is among the most commonly discussed low-cost appearance interventions in lifestyle communities, usually alongside veneers and orthodontics. T Nation threads mention whitening toothpaste and commercial strip products, and discussions of charcoal whitening have also appeared.[14][15]

Products differ in peroxide type (hydrogen or carbamide peroxide), concentration, wear time, strip shape and coverage, and whether they carry professional-body endorsements; product labels give the manufacturer's regimen and contraindications.

Randomized trials show peroxide whiteners lighten teeth compared with placebo: a 1992 double-blind trial of two carbamide peroxide products reported significantly whiter teeth than placebo at six weeks,[6] and a 2000 randomized controlled trial examined whitening efficacy and safety.[16] A 2007 trial compared strips, paint-on gel and a negative control.[9] A 2020 meta-analysis compared strips with supervised bleaching;[10] the 2018 Cochrane review covers home-based bleaching systems.[11] A 2024 randomized trial of activated-charcoal products examined their whitening efficacy,[17] and trials of in-office light-activated systems (violet LED) compare other techniques.[18] A 2014 review summarised research as showing whitening to be safe and effective when manufacturer protocols are followed, with risks to be aware of.[4]

lore.intro: Whitening strips appear on looksmax.org mainly in questions about safety and in product threads, and on T Nation in brief mentions of charcoal and whitening toothpaste.[19][21][14][15]

claims.claim: Whitening strips may damage teeth, so their safety is in doubt.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread opens by asking whether whitening strips damage teeth and whether they are safe to use.[19] Posters in related threads describe whitening as making teeth "very sensitive."[20]
claims.experts: A 2014 review summarised the research as showing whitening to be safe and effective when manufacturer protocols are followed, with transient tooth sensitivity and gum irritation the main side effects.[4][5] Wikipedia lists groups advised to use whitening with caution, including people with gum recession, exposed dentine or enamel defects.[1]

claims.claim: Using whitening strips during an isotretinoin (Accutane) course causes gum recession or discoloration.
claims.believers: One looksmax.org user reports gum recession starting on day 3 of strip use during isotretinoin treatment and says part of the gums stayed white for weeks. Another poster says the drying effect of isotretinoin could worsen sensitivity, while a third replies "no correlation."[20]
claims.experts: The sources reviewed contain no study of whitening during isotretinoin treatment. Wikipedia reports that gingival irritation is a recognised side effect of peroxide whitening and recommends a prior oral examination.[1]

claims.claim: Strips using PAP and charcoal instead of hydrogen peroxide whiten teeth effectively.
claims.believers: The author of a looksmax.org thread about a charcoal-and-PAP strip product, who says they had not yet tried it, points to before-and-after images from the maker's TikTok advertisement and to over 11,000 positive reviews. A replier says there will be "no difference."[21]
claims.experts: A 2024 single-blind randomized trial examined the whitening efficacy of activated-charcoal-based products.[17] Peroxide-based strips have been compared with placebo and with professional bleaching in randomized trials and reviews.[6][9][10][11]

claims.claim: Charcoal toothpaste whitening does irreversible harm to teeth.
claims.believers: In a T Nation thread, a poster who describes a dental background says people are using charcoal to brush their teeth as a "natural" whitening gimmick and that they tell them to stop because of irreversible damage.[14]
claims.experts: A 2024 randomized trial studied the whitening efficacy of activated-charcoal products.[17] Wikipedia describes whitening toothpastes as using abrasives and sometimes low-concentration peroxide.[1]
